hero.title: Test: are you ready
hero.description: 20 questions to assess your readiness for parenthood: emotional maturity, finances, relationship, lifestyle. An honest and kind stocktake.
hero.subtitle: Free, confidential, instant result

section1.title: The real signs of emotional maturity for becoming a parent
section1.p1: Emotional maturity isn't the absence of fear. It's the ability to recognise your fears, name them and move forward anyway. A future parent who is emotionally ready knows how to handle their own emotions before having to handle a newborn's at 3 in the morning. That comes down to several concrete things: being able to ask for help without shame, accepting that you can't control everything, and having made a minimum of peace with your own family history. Research in perinatal psychology shows that parents who have worked on their attachment style before a child arrives experience a calmer transition into parenthood. It isn't a question of perfection, it's a question of self-awareness. If you're able to step back from your reactions, apologise when you're wrong and tolerate emotional discomfort, you already have a solid base.

section2.title: Financial readiness: what does a baby really cost?
section2.p1: Let's talk numbers, because love doesn't pay for nappies. In most Western countries, a baby costs on average the equivalent of 500 to 800 euros a month in the first year: nappies, feeding, clothes, equipment, health costs not covered by insurance. And that's before childcare, which can easily double the bill. Being financially ready doesn't mean being wealthy. It means having a clear view of your income, your spending and your ability to absorb an additional cost without financial stress becoming permanent. Having a small savings cushion, knowing your entitlements (parental leave, family allowances, birth grants where they exist) and having thought through childcare are markers of realistic preparation. If your finances are fragile, that isn't a ban, it's a signal to shore things up before taking the plunge.

section3.title: A solid relationship: an indispensable foundation
section3.p1: A baby doesn't save a struggling relationship. That's a dangerous myth the statistics clearly contradict: according to a study in the Journal of Family Psychology, roughly 67% of couples see a drop in relationship satisfaction in the first three years after a birth. The couples who come through it best are those who already had solid communication, healthy conflict management and well-anchored mutual respect. Before considering a baby, ask yourself honestly: is your relationship in a good place? Can you argue without destroying each other? Does the wish for a child come from both of you, or mainly from one partner? Before a decision of that size, it is worth knowing what already holds and what doesn't: they are the same markers that make a relationship healthy.

section4.title: The lifestyle adjustments to anticipate
section4.p1: A baby doesn't slot into your current life, it transforms it. Lie-ins, spontaneous outings, quiet evenings, travelling light: all of that will change, at least for a while. This isn't meant to frighten you, it's meant to prepare you. The parents who handle the transition best are those who had realistic expectations. They knew the first six months would be a marathon of tiredness and adaptation. They had accepted the idea of putting some hobbies on hold. And above all, they didn't see those sacrifices as losses, but as conscious choices. In practical terms, think about your current daily rhythm. Is it compatible with a newborn's needs? If you live at full speed between work, sport and a social life, you'll need an adjustment period. And if you're thinking of moving in together, settle that question before the baby arrives, not at the same time.

section5.title: Career and parenthood: finding the right balance
section5.p1: The work question is often the one people put off the longest, and yet it weighs heavily on the decision. Maternity leave, paternity leave, returning to work, childcare, a possible reduction in hours: every choice has concrete implications for your daily life and your finances. Statutory leave varies a great deal from one country to another, and in every case it's a start, not a complete solution. The real question is what happens afterwards. Who goes back to work first? Who reduces their hours if needed? How do you handle the mental load of organising childcare? These conversations deserve to happen before the pregnancy, not during. Because the mental load, if it isn't anticipated and shared, becomes one of the first sources of tension in young families.

section6.title: Why a support network matters so much for new parents
section6.p1: You make a baby with two people, but you raise one with a village. That African proverb has never been more relevant. Studies show that social support is one of the strongest protective factors against parental burnout and postnatal depression. Having grandparents available, friends who've been through it, a kind neighbour: all of that counts enormously. If the people close to you are far away or not very available, that isn't a deal-breaker, but it needs compensating for. Identify the resources around you: new parent groups, breastfeeding support networks, local health services, online forums. The key is not to be left alone with a newborn and the feeling that you should be handling everything. Happy parenting runs on support, not on individual performance.

section7.title: Getting ready mentally: genuine desire versus social pressure
section7.p1: There's a fundamental difference between wanting a child and feeling obliged to want one. Social pressure, family pressure, the famous "so, when are you two having kids?", friends having one baby after another: all of it can blur the line between authentic desire and conformity. Before moving forward, take the time to ask yourself, alone with yourself: if nobody asked me the question, if nobody expected it, would I still want a child? The answer doesn't have to be an enthusiastic yes. It can be a "yes, but not now" or an "I need time to think about it". All of those answers are valid. What isn't valid is having a baby by default, under pressure or out of fear of missing the boat. A child deserves to arrive in a family that chose them, not in a family that gave in.

section8.title: The right moment vs the perfect moment: why perfection is a trap
section8.p1: If you wait for everything to line up perfectly before having a baby, you never will. The ideal home, the ideal salary, ideal maturity, the ideal relationship: that scenario only exists in films. In reality, the right moment is recognisable by a few concrete signals: your relationship is stable, your finances are sufficient (not necessarily comfortable), your desire is sincere and shared, and you feel able to face the unknown. That's it. The rest you'll learn along the way, like every parent before you. This parenthood test for couples can round out your thinking if you want to assess your readiness together. Because parenting is a team project, and the best teams are the ones that prepare for the match together, not the ones that improvise on the day.

seo.faq1Q: How do I know if I'm ready for a baby?
seo.faq1A: There's no universal checklist, but several indicators can guide you: sufficient emotional and financial stability, a sincere desire (not just one driven by social pressure), a solid relationship, an identified support network and the capacity to accept that your life is going to change profoundly. This test helps you assess these different aspects concretely.
seo.faq2Q: Is it normal to be afraid of having a baby?
seo.faq2A: Absolutely. Fear is in fact a sign of clear-sightedness: it shows you grasp the scale of what's ahead. A total absence of fear would be more worrying. What matters is that the fear isn't paralysing and that you can talk about it, with your partner, someone close or a professional. Expectant parents who dare to name their fears generally experience a smoother transition into parenthood.
seo.faq3Q: What's the right age to have a first child?
seo.faq3A: There's no universally ideal age. Medically, female fertility begins to decline after 35, but emotional maturity, financial stability and the quality of the relationship count just as much. Some couples at 25 are more ready than others at 38. The best indicator remains a sincere and shared desire, combined with a realistic capacity to welcome a child into your life.
seo.faq4Q: My partner doesn't want children, what should I do?
seo.faq4A: This is one of the most delicate disagreements in a relationship. The first step is to understand the nature of that refusal: is it a "not now" or a "never"? Open the conversation without pressure or ultimatums. If the subject stays blocked, a couples therapist can help you explore that gap in a neutral setting. Forcing or manipulating the other person is never an option, a child has to be wanted by both parents.
seo.faq5Q: Can a baby strengthen a fragile relationship?
seo.faq5A: No, and it's often the opposite. A baby amplifies the dynamics already present in a relationship: if communication is good, it can strengthen around the shared project. But if tensions exist, lack of sleep, stress and the mental load will make them worse. Studies show that the couples who hold up best after a birth are those who already had solid foundations. Before thinking about a baby, make sure your relationship is in good health.
